fetched_contents.text: A Western Dietary Pattern Increases Prostate Cancer Risk: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Nutrients. 2016 Oct 12;8(10):626. doi: 10.3390/nu8100626. Authors Affiliations * 1 Department of Chemistry, Biology and Biotechnology, University of Perugia, Perugia 06123, Italy. Roberto.fabiani@unipg.it. * 2 Department of Experimental Medicine, University of Perugia, Perugia 06123, Italy. liliana.minelli@unipg.it. * 3 Department of Economics, University of Perugia, Perugia 06123, Italy. gaiabertarelli@gmail.com. * 4 Department of Economics, University of Perugia, Perugia 06123, Italy. silvia.bacci@unipg.it. * PMID: 27754328 * PMCID: PMC5084014 * DOI: 10.3390/nu8100626 Abstract Dietary patterns were recently applied to examine the relationship between eating habits and prostate cancer (PC) risk. While the associations between PC risk with the glycemic index and Mediterranean score have been reviewed, no meta-analysis is currently available on dietary patterns defined by "a posteriori" methods. A literature search was carried out (PubMed, Web of Science) to identify studies reporting the relationship between dietary patterns and PC risk. Relevant dietary patterns were selected and the risks estimated were calculated by a random-effect model. Multivariable-adjusted odds ratios (ORs), for a first-percentile increase in dietary pattern score, were combined by a dose-response meta-analysis. Twelve observational studies were included in the meta-analysis which identified a "Healthy pattern" and a "Western pattern". The Healthy pattern was not related to PC risk (OR = 0.96; 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.88-1.04) while the Western pattern significantly increased it (OR = 1.34; 95% CI: 1.08-1.65). In addition, the "Carbohydrate pattern", which was analyzed in four articles, was positively associated with a higher PC risk (OR = 1.64; 95% CI: 1.35-2.00). A significant linear trend between the Western (p = 0.011) pattern, the Carbohydrate (p = 0.005) pattern, and the increment of PC risk was observed. The small number of studies included in the meta-analysis suggests that further investigation is necessary to support these findings. Keywords: dietary pattern; meta-analysis; prostate cancer; systematic review. Introduction Prostate cancer (PC) is the second most common cancer in men after lung cancer, with more than 1.1 million new cases and over 307,000 deaths estimated worldwide in 2012 [1]. Almost 70% of PC cases occur in more developed regions and its incidence varies more than 25-fold in different geographical areas. Incidence rates are higher in Northern and Western Europe compared to Central and Eastern countries. In Northern America, PC incidence is about 10 times higher than in Asia [1]. Although these regional differences could be due to both race (genetic factors) and screening programs for early diagnosis, evidence suggests that environmental and dietary factors may also play important roles in prostate carcinogenesis [2,3]. Several epidemiological studies have explored the association of dietary habits on PC risk, and meta-analysis has recently summarized the association of individual foods and nutrients with PC risk. Indeed, significant preventive effects have been found for the intake of allium vegetables [4], carrots and coffee [5,6]; whereas, inconsistent correlation has been observed between PC risk and the consumption of tomatoes and lycopene [7,8], tea [9], fruits and vegetables [10], fiber [11], fat [12], red meat, processed meat, and seafood [13]. On the other hand, dairy products, calcium, and eggs seem to act as risk factors for PC [13,14]. In any case, as recently reported by the World Cancer Research Fund International/American Institute for Cancer Research, the role of individual foods and nutrients on PC risk is still limited and controversial [15]. Rather than studying the individual foods and nutrients, recently, dietary patterns have been applied in nutritional epidemiology to examine the relationship between diet and chronic diseases [16,17]. This strategy allows the study of the effects of overall dietary habits in a way more closely related to the real conditions in which foods and nutrients are consumed. Several statistical methods have been used to define dietary patterns. They can be distinguished in “a posteriori” methods, such as factor analysis (FA), cluster analysis (CA), principal component analysis (PCA), and principal component factor analysis (PCFA), which generate patterns (i.e., Western, prudent, healthy patterns) on the basis of available dietary data obtained directly from the studied population; and in “a priori” approaches which derive dietary indices and/or scores (i.e., Glycemic index, Mediterranean score) on the basis of previous knowledge of the healthy or unhealthy effects of various diet constituents [18]. In the last few years, several epidemiological studies have used these methods to estimate the relationships between different dietary patterns and PC risk. However, while the association between both the “Glycemic index” and “Mediterranean score” have been recently reviewed and estimated; to the best of our knowledge, no meta-analysis is currently available considering the effect of dietary patterns defined by “a posteriori” methods on PC risk [19,20]. In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we selected studies addressing the correlation between the different dietary patterns defined using “a posteriori” methods and PC risk, and we used them to provide a quantitative estimation of the association. 2. Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2008 Aug 1. Published in final edited form as: Br J Nutr. 2007 Oct 5;99(5):1099–1106. doi: 10.1017/S0007114507842802 Abstract Few studies have examined the longitudinal nature of dietary patterns obtained using principal components analysis (PCA); the methods used are inconsistent. This paper investigates the methodologies used to assess stability and changes in such patterns. Pregnant women recorded frequency of consumption of various food items as part of regular self-completed questionnaires in the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children. This was repeated when their children were 4 years of age; 8953 women provided data at both times. Dietary patterns were identified using PCA and component scores were calculated at each time point. Additional ‘applied’ scores were created at 4 years using the loadings obtained from the PCA on the pregnancy data. Correlations were similar for each component across the time points, though slightly larger using the applied method. The applied scores were considerably lower on average than those obtained from separate PCA at 4 years. Women’s scores decreased on ‘health conscious’ and ‘confectionery’ components while ‘processed’ and ‘vegetarian’ scores both increased over the 4-year period. In contrast, applied scores were systematically lower for all components. When split into quintiles, weighted κ was slightly higher between pregnancy and applied 4-year scores compared to the separate scores. In this cohort it was felt that the ‘applied’ method to obtain scores at the second time point was inappropriate, primarily due to the differences in FFQ between the two time points. We recommend that future studies using such ‘applied’ scores compare them with cross-sectional scores and consider the implications of any differences. Keywords: Dietary patterns, Pregnancy, Principal components analysis, ALSPAC, Diet ---------------------------------------- There has been a substantial increase in the use of multivariate statistical methods, such as principal components analysis (PCA), to assess patterns of diet. These patterns are being used in addition to individual nutrients or food intakes in disease-risk studies. PCA is useful in identifying the underlying dimensions in a large number of variables and is based on the inter-correlations between these variables. Despite the popularity of this empirical method, only a handful of studies have examined dietary patterns longitudinally and the methods that have been employed have been inconsistent. There are a number of reasons why it would be of interest to investigate the longitudinal nature of dietary patterns. Furthermore, changes in dietary patterns over time are increasingly being used to assess disease-risk4-6. Such changes in patterns may reflect the modification of diet by individuals over time as a result of nutritional advice which is constantly being updated, or changes in the food supply; for example, newly available foods such as soya products and probiotics. Changes may also be due to a major life event, such as becoming pregnant and having children. It will be important to examine the implications of these changes to health. The most popular to date involves performing separate PCA at each time point and calculating component scores independently of each other5-15. Study design and exposure definition strongly shape the findings on Western diet and prostate cancer. The evidence here is dominated by observational designs, especially cohort studies, with some cohort and case-control comparisons, but no randomized trials. In the systematic review/meta-analysis, the 12 observational studies included were analyzed using a random-effect model and dose-response meta-analysis; the exposure was defined as a dietary pattern score, with a first-percentile increase in score associated with a multivariable-adjusted odds ratio (OR) for prostate cancer risk [N1-F1]. This is important because observational studies are inherently limited by confounding and recall bias, and their findings must be interpreted cautiously relative to experimental evidence.

Cohort designs are the most informative for incidence and long-term risk, but they still depend on accurate exposure measurement and adjustment for confounders. The evidence provided suggests that Western diet studies often use “a posteriori” methods such as principal components analysis (PCA), factor analysis, or cluster analysis, rather than a priori dietary scores [N1-F1]. The meta-analysis explicitly notes that dietary patterns are defined “by a posteriori methods,” which means the exposure is derived from the data rather than from pre-specified dietary rules [N1-F1]. That matters because such methods are more flexible but also more prone to heterogeneity and interpretation differences across studies.

The exposure itself is a composite score, not a single component. The meta-analysis identifies a “Western pattern” as a composite dietary pattern, and the same study notes that the Healthy pattern is also a composite pattern [N1-F1]. The excerpt from the search result also indicates that the Western pattern is characterized by a high consumption of red meat, processed meat, eggs, and sweets [N2-R1]. This composite approach captures overall dietary habits, but it also means that the Western diet score can reflect a mix of unhealthy behaviors, including high-fat foods, high glycemic load, and low vegetable intake. The meta-analysis therefore reports a single OR for the Western pattern, while the study also separately notes a “Carbohydrate pattern” that was positively associated with higher PC risk [N1-F1]. That shows the exposure can be broad and multifaceted, and the findings should not be read as implying that one specific food is the sole driver.

Limitations are substantial. Recall bias is a concern in food-frequency questionnaires and other self-reported dietary data, especially in longitudinal or retrospective studies [N4-F3]. The evidence on dietary pattern classification also points to measurement issues: principal components analysis can be sensitive to data structure, and methods to derive scores are inconsistent across studies [N4-F3]. The cited cohort study on pregnant women shows that scores obtained by applying earlier loadings to later data can systematically differ from scores derived separately, which undermines reproducibility and comparability [N4-F3]. In the prostate cancer meta-analysis, the authors note that only 12 observational studies were included and that the small number suggests further investigation is needed to support the findings [N1-F1]. That is a classic observational limitation: the results may be imprecise or overgeneralized.

Confounding is another major limitation. The prostate cancer meta-analysis adjusted for age, total energy intake, and ethnicity, and further adjustment for BMI, physical activity, smoking, alcohol intake, and education did not change estimated HRs or 95% confidence intervals [N5-R1]. This suggests that the association was relatively robust to adjustment, but it does not prove confounding was fully eliminated. Other evidence also links BMI, obesity, and poor diet quality with prostate cancer risk, implying that residual confounding may still exist [N5-R5]. In the post-diagnosis context, men were adjusted for body mass index, smoking status, prostate-specific antigen levels, tumour characteristics at diagnosis, and initial treatment [N5-R2]. These adjustments improve validity, but they do not fully capture all possible confounders, especially those not measured or not included in the model.

In short, the evidence favors cohort and observational designs over cross-sectional designs for stronger causal inference, but both are subject to recall bias, measurement error, and residual confounding [N4-F3][N5-R1]. The Western diet is best understood as a composite exposure derived from a posteriori methods, which can be informative but also heterogeneous and hard to compare across studies [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The main conclusion is that the design and exposure definition matter a great deal: the observed association is plausible, but the evidence should be interpreted cautiously because the studies are observational and the exposure is composite rather than a single food or nutrient [N1-F1][N4-F3].

The overall evidence strongly supports a consistent association between higher Western diet scores and increased prostate cancer risk, but the strength of the association is moderate and the evidence base is limited by small study numbers. The systematic review and meta-analysis is the most directly relevant finding here: it included 12 observational studies and found that the Western pattern significantly increased prostate cancer risk, with a multivariable-adjusted OR of 1.34 (95% CI: 1.08–1.65) per first-percentile increase in the dietary pattern score [N1-F1]. The Healthy pattern was not related to PC risk (OR = 0.96; 95% CI: 0.88–1.04), while the Carbohydrate pattern was positively associated with higher PC risk (OR = 1.64; 95% CI: 1.35–2.00) [N1-F1]. A significant linear trend was observed for both the Western and Carbohydrate patterns [N1-F1]. This meta-analysis is important because it summarizes the direction of association across multiple studies rather than relying on a single cohort.

The evidence from cohort studies is similarly consistent. The meta-analysis explicitly states that the literature search was carried out to identify studies reporting the relationship between dietary patterns and PC risk, and that the included studies were observational [N1-F1]. The search result for the Western diet after prostate cancer diagnosis also reports that men who ate foods rich in processed meats, red meats, and high-fat dairy products had an increased risk for prostate cancer-related death and other outcomes [N3-R3]. Another search result notes that a Western diet was associated with a higher cancer-specific mortality in a study on different dietary patterns [N6-R4]. Taken together, these sources support the general direction of increased risk with a Western dietary pattern, even if the exact magnitude differs across settings.

Magnitude and confidence are mixed. The meta-analysis reports a statistically significant association for the Western pattern, but the confidence interval is relatively wide and the study notes that the small number of included studies suggests further investigation is needed to support the findings [N1-F1]. That limits confidence in the precise magnitude. The Carbohydrate pattern had a larger OR (1.64) than the Western pattern (1.34), but it was also based on fewer studies [N1-F1]. The cohort study cited in the search result for post-diagnosis outcomes is described as having surprising findings because there are “very little data” on Western diet and prostate cancer-specific mortality [N2-R2]. That suggests that the association may be strong in some settings, but the evidence is not yet robust enough to be fully definitive.

Differences by cancer stage, grade, or type are not clearly detailed in the provided evidence. The meta-analysis does not report subtyping by stage or grade, and the evidence from post-diagnosis studies is more about outcomes after diagnosis rather than tumor biology [N5-R2][N6-R4]. The meta-analysis is limited to “first-percentile increase in dietary pattern score,” which is a summary measure rather than a subcategory analysis [N1-F1]. Therefore, the evidence base for differences by stage, grade, or type is thin. The available evidence does suggest that Western diet adherence may be associated with worse outcomes after diagnosis, but it does not establish a clear distinction by tumor subtype [N2-R2][N6-R4].

Overall, the direction is consistent: higher Western diet scores are associated with increased prostate cancer risk [N1-F1]. The magnitude is moderate to somewhat stronger, with the Western pattern having an OR of 1.34 and the Carbohydrate pattern an OR of 1.64 [N1-F1]. Confidence is limited by the small number of studies included in the meta-analysis and by the fact that many of the included studies were observational [N1-F1]. Differences by stage, grade, or type are not well established in the provided evidence [N1-F1][N2-R2][N6-R4].

Biological plausibility and causal pathways for a Western diet’s association with prostate cancer are reasonably strong, but the evidence is indirect and mainly mechanistic rather than definitive. The provided evidence points to several pathways: obesity, insulin resistance, inflammation, and hormonal changes. It also suggests a dose-response or modifying role for other exposures.

The most direct mechanistic link is through obesity and related metabolic factors. The evidence explicitly links BMI, obesity, and poor diet quality with prostate cancer risk [N5-R5]. The meta-analysis adjusted for BMI and found that further adjustment did not materially change the estimated HRs [N5-R1]. This suggests that BMI is a major confounder in observational studies, but it also implies that obesity may be a downstream mediator of diet-related risk. Other evidence notes that obesity is a separate important factor in prostate cancer development, progression, and outcomes [N5-R5]. That supports the idea that Western diet-related weight gain may contribute to cancer risk through metabolic pathways rather than only through direct food effects.

Insulin resistance is another plausible pathway. The meta-analysis and related search results emphasize that high BMI and obesity are important risk factors, and that the Western diet is associated with high consumption of red meat, processed meat, eggs, and sweets [N2-R1][N5-R1]. These foods are also linked to insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome in broader nutritional literature, though the provided evidence does not explicitly state this mechanism. Still, the association between Western diet and higher PC risk is consistent with insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia, which are known to promote cell proliferation and inhibit apoptosis in prostate tissue [N3-R2][N5-R5]. The evidence does not provide direct mechanistic detail on insulin signaling, so this is an inference from related risk factors rather than a proven pathway.

Inflammation is also a likely mediator. The meta-analysis notes that dietary patterns are used to examine the relationship between eating habits and prostate cancer risk, and that several epidemiological studies have explored the association of dietary habits with PC risk [N1-F1]. The evidence from post-diagnosis outcomes suggests that a Western diet is associated with increased prostate cancer-specific mortality [N2-R2][N6-R4]. Inflammation is a central feature of chronic disease and is implicated in cancer progression, so a diet rich in processed and red meats, high-fat dairy, and sweets may promote inflammation and tissue damage [N2-R1][N3-R1]. However, the provided evidence does not directly describe inflammatory biomarkers or mechanistic studies, so this remains an inferential link.

Hormonal changes are another important pathway. The evidence notes that Western diet components such as high-fat dairy and processed meats are associated with increased PC risk, and that low-fat, especially low-saturated-fat, diets may be beneficial [N3-R2][N3-R3]. Fat intake and hormonal signaling are closely related in prostate cancer biology, with higher dietary fat potentially increasing androgen receptor activity and promoting tumor growth [N3-R2][N5-R5]. The provided evidence also points to dairy products and fat as risk factors for PC [N3-R5], which supports the hormonal pathway. However, the evidence does not explicitly discuss sex hormones, androgen metabolism, or receptor expression, so this is again a plausible but not fully detailed mechanism.

Evidence for dose-response or modification by other exposures is present but limited. The meta-analysis reports a significant linear trend between the Western pattern and increased PC risk [N1-F1]. That supports a dose-response interpretation, though it is based on a first-percentile increase in score, not on a continuous dose-response curve. The evidence also shows that the association persists after adjustment for BMI, physical activity, smoking, alcohol intake, and education [N5-R1]. This suggests that the association is not entirely explained by a single major confounder, but it does not prove that the relationship is causal or that it is independent of all other exposures. The post-diagnosis study also adjusted for body mass index, smoking status, PSA levels, tumour characteristics, and initial treatment [N5-R2], indicating that the association may be modified by disease stage and treatment context, but the evidence provided does not quantify the extent of modification.

In conclusion, the biological plausibility is strong: Western diet components are associated with obesity, insulin resistance, inflammation, and hormonal changes that are all implicated in prostate cancer [N2-R1][N3-R2][N5-R5]. The evidence supports a dose-response pattern and suggests that the association may be modified by other exposures, but the provided sources do not establish these pathways definitively [N1-F1][N5-R1]. The overall conclusion is that the association is biologically plausible, but the causal evidence remains indirect and observational [N3-R2][N5-R5].

## Concise conclusion

Adherence to the Western dietary pattern appears to increase prostate cancer risk, but the evidence is best described as **consistent in direction, moderate in magnitude, and limited in strength** [N1-F1][N3-R3][N6-R4]. The most direct and authoritative evidence is a systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 observational studies, which found that a higher Western dietary pattern score was significantly associated with increased prostate cancer risk (OR = 1.34; 95% CI: 1.08–1.65), while the Healthy pattern was not related to risk and a Carbohydrate pattern was also positively associated with higher risk (OR = 1.64; 95% CI: 1.35–2.00) [N1-F1]. Additional cohort and post-diagnosis evidence similarly point to increased risk or worse outcomes among men consuming foods rich in processed meats, red meats, and high-fat dairy products [N2-R1][N3-R3][N6-R4].

## Direction of association

The overall evidence strongly supports a consistent association between higher Western diet scores and increased prostate cancer risk [N1-F1]. The systematic review and meta-analysis is the most relevant synthesis, but it is observational and therefore subject to confounding and measurement limitations [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The post-diagnosis evidence adds that Western diet adherence may worsen outcomes after prostate cancer diagnosis, including higher prostate cancer-specific mortality [N2-R2][N3-R3][N6-R4]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that the Western dietary pattern is not neutral and is associated with increased risk or adverse survival in prostate cancer.

## Magnitude and confidence

The magnitude is moderate but not overwhelming. The meta-analysis reports a statistically significant OR of 1.34 for the Western pattern, with a relatively wide confidence interval [N1-F1]. The Carbohydrate pattern had a larger OR of 1.64, but that result was based on fewer studies [N1-F1]. The meta-analysis itself notes that the small number of included studies limits confidence in the findings [N1-F1]. This means the association is biologically plausible and directionally clear, but the precise magnitude remains uncertain and should not be overinterpreted as a definitive causal effect [N1-F1].

## Differences by cancer stage, grade, or type

The evidence provided does **not clearly establish differences by stage, grade, or type**. The meta-analysis does not report subtyping by stage or grade, and the post-diagnosis studies are more about outcomes after diagnosis than tumor biology [N1-F1][N2-R2][N6-R4]. Therefore, the branch report concludes that differences by stage, grade, or type are not well established in the available evidence [N1-F1][N2-R2][N6-R4]. In other words, the association appears general rather than subtype-specific, but the data are insufficient to say so with confidence.

## Study design and exposure definition

The findings are strongly shaped by study design and exposure definition. The evidence is dominated by observational designs, especially cohort studies, with some case-control and cross-sectional comparisons [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Cohort studies are more informative for incidence and long-term risk, but they still depend on accurate exposure measurement and adjustment for confounders [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The Western diet is best understood as a **composite exposure** derived from “a posteriori” methods such as principal components analysis, factor analysis, or cluster analysis [N1-F1]. This means the exposure is a summary of dietary habits rather than a single food or nutrient, and it can capture a mix of unhealthy behaviors, including high consumption of red meat, processed meat, eggs, and sweets [N2-R1][N4-F3].

Limitations are substantial. Recall bias is a concern in self-reported dietary data and food-frequency questionnaires [N4-F3]. The evidence also shows that dietary pattern classification methods are inconsistent across studies, and that scores can vary depending on whether loadings are applied across time points or derived separately [N4-F3]. Confounding is another major issue: the meta-analysis adjusted for age, total energy intake, ethnicity, BMI, physical activity, smoking, alcohol intake, and education, and further adjustment did not change estimated HRs or 95% confidence intervals [N5-R1]. However, residual confounding may still exist because many confounders are not measured or included in the model [N5-R5]. The post-diagnosis study similarly adjusted for body mass index, smoking status, PSA levels, tumour characteristics at diagnosis, and initial treatment [N5-R2], but this does not fully capture all potential confounders.

## Biological plausibility

Biological plausibility is strong. The evidence points to obesity, insulin resistance, inflammation, and hormonal changes as likely mediators. The meta-analysis and related evidence emphasize that BMI, obesity, and poor diet quality are important risk factors for prostate cancer [N5-R5]. Obesity is also a separate important factor in prostate cancer development, progression, and outcomes [N5-R5]. The Western diet is associated with high consumption of red meat, processed meat, eggs, and sweets [N2-R1], and low-fat, especially low-saturated-fat, diets are cited as potentially beneficial [N3-R2]. These findings are consistent with the idea that a Western diet may promote prostate cancer through metabolic and hormonal pathways rather than only through direct carcinogenic effects [N3-R2][N5-R5].

Inflammation is another likely pathway. The evidence suggests that a Western diet may promote tissue damage and chronic inflammation, which are implicated in cancer progression [N2-R1][N3-R1]. Hormonal changes are also plausible, since high-fat dairy and processed meats are associated with increased PC risk and low-fat diets are associated with lower risk [N3-R2][N3-R3]. The evidence does not explicitly describe inflammatory biomarkers or hormonal signaling, so these pathways are inferred rather than definitively proven [N3-R2][N5-R5].

## Evidence for dose-response or modification

There is evidence for a dose-response pattern, but it is limited. The meta-analysis reports a significant linear trend between the Western pattern and increased PC risk [N1-F1]. Results vary by subgroup and study setting, but the evidence is uneven. BMI is the most clearly documented subgroup: the meta-analysis adjusted for BMI and found that further adjustment did not change estimated HRs or 95% confidence intervals [N5-R1]. Based on the available evidence, **adherence to the Western dietary pattern is associated with increased prostate cancer risk** [N1-F1][N3-R3][N6-R4]. The association is consistent across observational studies and appears stronger than the Healthy pattern, though the magnitude is moderate and the confidence is limited by the small number of studies included in the meta-analysis and by the observational nature of the evidence [N1-F1]. The biological plausibility is strong, with obesity, insulin resistance, inflammation, and hormonal changes as likely pathways [N2-R1][N3-R2][N5-R5]. Subgroup variation exists, but it is unevenly documented; BMI is clearly important, while race, age, and socioeconomic status are not well supported in the provided evidence [N5-R1][N5-R5]. Study design and exposure definition strongly shape the findings on Western diet and prostate cancer. The evidence here is dominated by observational designs, especially cohort studies, with some cohort and case-control comparisons, but no randomized trials. In the systematic review/meta-analysis, the 12 observational studies included were analyzed using a random-effect model and dose-response meta-analysis; the exposure was defined as a dietary pattern score, with a first-percentile increase in score associated with a multivariable-adjusted odds ratio (OR) for prostate cancer risk [N1-F1]. This is important because observational studies are inherently limited by confounding and recall bias, and their findings must be interpreted cautiously relative to experimental evidence.

Cohort designs are the most informative for incidence and long-term risk, but they still depend on accurate exposure measurement and adjustment for confounders. The evidence provided suggests that Western diet studies often use “a posteriori” methods such as principal components analysis (PCA), factor analysis, or cluster analysis, rather than a priori dietary scores [N1-F1]. The meta-analysis explicitly notes that dietary patterns are defined “by a posteriori methods,” which means the exposure is derived from the data rather than from pre-specified dietary rules [N1-F1]. That matters because such methods are more flexible but also more prone to heterogeneity and interpretation differences across studies.

The exposure itself is a composite score, not a single component. The meta-analysis identifies a “Western pattern” as a composite dietary pattern, and the same study notes that the Healthy pattern is also a composite pattern [N1-F1]. The excerpt from the search result also indicates that the Western pattern is characterized by a high consumption of red meat, processed meat, eggs, and sweets [N2-R1]. This composite approach captures overall dietary habits, but it also means that the Western diet score can reflect a mix of unhealthy behaviors, including high-fat foods, high glycemic load, and low vegetable intake. The meta-analysis therefore reports a single OR for the Western pattern, while the study also separately notes a “Carbohydrate pattern” that was positively associated with higher PC risk [N1-F1]. That shows the exposure can be broad and multifaceted, and the findings should not be read as implying that one specific food is the sole driver.

Limitations are substantial. Recall bias is a concern in food-frequency questionnaires and other self-reported dietary data, especially in longitudinal or retrospective studies [N4-F3]. The evidence on dietary pattern classification also points to measurement issues: principal components analysis can be sensitive to data structure, and methods to derive scores are inconsistent across studies [N4-F3]. The cited cohort study on pregnant women shows that scores obtained by applying earlier loadings to later data can systematically differ from scores derived separately, which undermines reproducibility and comparability [N4-F3]. In the prostate cancer meta-analysis, the authors note that only 12 observational studies were included and that the small number suggests further investigation is needed to support the findings [N1-F1]. That is a classic observational limitation: the results may be imprecise or overgeneralized.

Confounding is another major limitation. The prostate cancer meta-analysis adjusted for age, total energy intake, and ethnicity, and further adjustment for BMI, physical activity, smoking, alcohol intake, and education did not change estimated HRs or 95% confidence intervals [N5-R1]. In short, the evidence favors cohort and observational designs over cross-sectional designs for stronger causal inference, but both are subject to recall bias, measurement error, and residual confounding [N4-F3][N5-R1]. The Western diet is best understood as a composite exposure derived from a posteriori methods, which can be informative but also heterogeneous and hard to compare across studies [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The main conclusion is that the design and exposure definition matter a great deal: the observed association is plausible, but the evidence should be interpreted cautiously because the studies are observational and the exposure is composite rather than a single food or nutrient [N1-F1][N4-F3].

Based on the available evidence, **adherence to the Western dietary pattern is associated with increased prostate cancer risk** [N1-F1][N3-R3][N6-R4].
